Wednesday P. Mo Oct. 27, 9
1937.
Section 2.
Dear Family:
Its 9 P.M. Mr. Bond and I have just boarded the good ship Kung Wo
at Hankow.
We each have a large spacious cabin and we are both turning in before
the ship sails.
We have had another busy day trying all day to make our Chinese
associates understand a business proposal which would be guite easy for a twelve
year old child to master in half an hour. Such work is what ages one in Chine.
The men to whom we were talking represent the type with whom we must do business.
It would try the patience of Job. After a dey of such negotiations you are com-
pletely worn out.
Thursday Oct. 28th. Have just been ashore at Kiukiang to look see
China shops.
Bought two small porcelain pictures just to have something purchased
where the best modern porcelain is made. All day we have travelled along the broad
Yangtze stopping anly at Anking about six o'clock P.M. There we anchored and a
huge sampan - alive with Chinese came alongside, tied up to our boat while an fast
a scene of utmost chaos a hugh amount of practicably worthless cargo came on board
including about 100 coolies.
An approximately similer number got off with an in-
ferno of walla walla md onfusion of small baskets, bundles and boxes. Four youg
wounded soldiers were interesting. They were Nenking boys wounded in the fighting
in the north and were being sent back to their failies in Nanking. None of them
looked to be over sixteen years old.
There are only Bur first class passengers on this large river boat -
the other two are Chinese, one bound for Wuhu where we land early tomorrow morn-
ing and the other for Chinking, a town just upstream from the boom which the
Chinese have stretched across the Yangisze to keep the Jap fleet out of the river.
Our Captain and his first mate - both Britishers - say the boom is an effective
bar to navigation. It is composed of old hulks filled with stones and sunk side
by side clear across the river. Below the boom an extensive system of mines makes
it dangerous to even approach the boom. The small Chinese boats can get around
the boom through a series of canals and are busy carrying Shanghai cargo around
the boom, which cergo is delivered then to English boats which carry it in either
direction to or away from Shanghai.
Friday, Oct. 29th.
Went to bed at 9 P.M. and didn't wake up until 8 A.
so you see I'm not suffering from insomnia. This morning there is a cold wind blow-
ing from the north. We have just left Wuhu and are due at Nanking about noon.
The weather is bad - which is good - because the Japs can't bomb with a low ceiling.
If they fly low the enti-aircraft guns shoot them down and if they fly high they
can't see Nenking because there is a solid overcast at about 3000 feet. Also since
International r essure has been exerted against indiscriminate bombing that type of
attack has been practiced only against cities and towns where there are no influen-
tial foreigners.
Sat. Oct. 30th.
We arrived Nanking without incident. The boat docked
about three miles upstream from the Nanking Bund and we transferred to a tug which
brought us (standing in the Kain on front deck) to the dock. There we hired the
most disreputable looking old Ford taxi end set out for the American Embassy. The
main drag (Chung Shen Road) is lined with bomb shelters.
Otherwise the capital
quiet and untouched by war as before the present hostilities began.
Several bomb sears have since been pointed out to me but craters have been filled
and no signs of damage are discernible.
None of the large public buildings has
been hit though many have been the target of air raids.
We are living at the
American Embassy with Mr. Peck who very kindly invited us to live with him during
our stay in Nanking. Last night Mr. Peck had a dinner party with Ambassador
Johnson, a Dr. and Mrs. Hershberg and their twenty year old daughter.
They were
very charming Germans who all poke excellent English. Dr. Hershberg is a famous
surgeon who hes done some remarkable operations and is helping tremendously in
the present Chinese hospital management. It is suspected that he left a good prac-
tice in Germany to avo id persecution by Hittlerites. After dinner we played

"Poker Patience". There wes no bomb raids as the bad weather continued.
Sunday A.M. Oct. 31st. Yesterday was also a bad day - therefore a good
day. Our Managing Director arrived from Hankow having been unable to join us
Friday because the airplane schedule was cancelled that day account weether.
Vie
had a session with him - went to dinner at the International Club where most of the
foreigners remaining in Nanking congregate every Saturday night to make a little
whoopie up to curfew time at 11 P.M.
I met many old friends there and hed a fine
time.
There was only one woman present - a French girl who arrived here a few
weeks
ago as a volunteer nurse - fell in love with a French newspaper errespondes
and was married night before last.
The whole town turned out for the wedding.
Women in Manking are so scarce that whenever you see one you stamp your hand
the kids do when they see a white horse. About 80% of the foreign population of
Wanking has gone.
I had a long talk with Mr. Holm e good friend of ours who used to be Posta
Commissioner at Chungking.
He has resigned and is keen on returning with Mrs. Holm
to his "home" in Copenhagen ofter thirty years in China. I wonder if they won't
soon went to come back.
Here, for instance, at Chungking Mr. Holm was a real per-
sonage. He lived in a beautiful Chinese house (provided rent free by the Post
surrounded by a lovely garden. He travelled to work in a grand sedan chair
fitted out like a small throne, borne by Bur uniformed chair coolies. He had a
No. 1 boy who ran the house and looked after every detail from food to pressing
his suits and shining his shoes. Several coolies were st his beek and oall to run
errands, bring him whatever he called for, eto. Three gardners cared for his
as though it were there own. It will be different in Copenhagen.
Later - Sunday night - rain end low ceiling all day. Had long conference
with Vice-Minister of Communications which lasted all morning and accomplished
nothing. Very discoursging.
Lunch with Ir. Peek and ir. Johnson also d inner -
much conversation but no results.
Americen attitude very sympathetic end helpful
Chinese very unsympathetic and non cooperative. Some Chinese officials can be
unbelievably dull and stupid. Our friend of today's onference seems intent only
on immediate necessities to the exclusion of all else. Hope for better luck to-
We have been here now two and one half days with no eir attack which probably
means a strong one or more tomorrow, unless
of course this weather continues. There
is an air of expectancy in lanking, a sort of indefinite tenseness which must get
on everyones' nerves sooner or later. Possibly they get used to it and probably
I would too but frankly I'll be glad to get away.
W11 send this letter by Tuesday's plane to Bankow with the hope that it
will catch Eurasia to Hongkong Wednesday and the Clipper to Manile on Thursday.
Next installment will B llow later.
We get little news here except about the Shanghei front and even that is
mixed with all sorts of wild rumors.
Weren't the Japs showing their real nature
when they fired at the "doomed battled on" when they evacueted that warehouse and
surrendered to the British for internment? Those dirty little Japs haven't any
decent traits.
Why didn't they cease firing and give those Chinese a rousing cheer
when they evacuated. That would have been sporting - but not at all Japanese.
As ever
Herold
